items.title: New EU deforestation law
items.text: The EU’s anti-deforestation law faces an enforcement test ahead of its launch on 30 December 2026. Under the new rules, companies selling goods such as palm oil, coffee, and cocoa must prove their products are not linked to land cleared after 2020. However, recent investigations by Indonesian environmental organizations reveal that major international consumer brands risk breaching these regulations. Reports show that companies like PepsiCo, Unilever, and Ferrero have bought palm oil from Indonesian plantations accused of recent illegal deforestation. Despite heavy political pressure and lobbying from major exporting nations like the United States and Indonesia to delay or soften the legislation, environmental activists insist the EU must strictly enforce the rules. Indonesia has lost vast areas of forest to illegal logging and agricultural clearing, which increased its vulnerability to severe wildfires. Experts emphasize that strict enforcement by European authorities will be essential to hold global corporations accountable and halt worldwide forest destruction. Difficult words: enforcement (compelling compliance with a law), lobby (to influence a politician or public official on an issue), vulnerability (the possibility of being attacked, damaged, or harmed). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: New EU deforestation law
items.text: The EU will start using new anti-deforestation rules on 30 December 2026. Companies which sell products like palm oil, coffee, and chocolate must prove they don’t cut down trees to make them. But environmental groups in Indonesia found that big international brands may be breaking these rules. Well-known companies like PepsiCo and Unilever recently bought palm oil from plantations linked to illegal forest clearing. Some countries, including the US and Indonesia, asked the EU to make the rules easier for businesses. But environmental activists say Europe must stay strong and enforce the law. Indonesia lost many forests to farming and fires, so strict checks are needed to protect nature and stop global forest destruction. Difficult words: anti-deforestation (about preventing or stopping the clearing of forests), brand (a product made by a company under a particular name), enforce (to make sure that a rule is followed). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: New EU deforestation law
items.text: The EU has a new rule to save forests. The rule is starting on 30 December 2026. Companies which sell things like coffee, palm oil, and chocolate must prove that they do not cut down trees. But some big companies are still buying palm oil from places in Indonesia. People cut down forests illegally there. Some countries want Europe to stop or change the rule. These countries are, for example, the US and Indonesia. But the EU must follow the rules strictly . Indonesia is losing many trees to big fires and farming. People hope that this new rule will stop companies from harming trees and help keep the earth green and safe. Difficult words: prove (to show that something is true), illegally (against rules), strictly (exactly). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Chinese baby companies have problems
items.text: Chinese companies that produce children’s products are diversifying their offerings to include adult and pet clothing, as the country faces a record-low birth rate that is expected to continue declining. The demographic decline can be traced back to China’s one-child policy, which lasted from 1980 to 2015. While the limit has been raised to three children in 2021, couples are still reluctant to have babies. Yan Zhang, founder and CEO of Shanghai children’s clothing brand NATUNAKIDS, said the company’s sales have not been significantly impacted by the low birth rate yet but he expects sales to decrease over the next three to five years. The shift in the industry has left some consumers worried about their favorite brands going bankrupt. Market analyst Shaun Rein warns that companies in the baby industry will face declining margins , bad revenues , and falling stock prices. Difficult words: reluctant (unwilling to do something), margin (profit), revenue (income). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Chinese baby companies have problems
items.text: Chinese companies that make products for children are expanding their product lines to include adult and pet clothing. The country’s falling birth rate is a result of the one-child policy that lasted from 1980 to 2015. The government raised the limit to three children in 2021, but couples are still not having babies. Yan Zhang, CEO of Shanghai children’s clothing brand NATUNAKIDS, expects sales to go down in the next three to five years. Customers worry that their favorite brands may go bankrupt as a result of the changes in the industry. Experts predict a bad future for baby companies in China. Difficult words: birth rate (how many children are born in a country in one year), brand (the name of products by one company), bankrupt (when a person or company has no money at all). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Chinese baby companies have problems
items.text: In China, fewer children are born every year. This starts in 1980 when the government says that people can only have one child. Now, companies which make things for kids are having problems. In 2021, the government says that families can have three children. But people do not want them. Companies start clothes for adults and pets instead of products for babies. Experts believe that sales of these companies will go down in the next few years. People who like certain brands worry that the companies will end. Experts say that baby companies will have a hard time in the future. Difficult words: pet (an animal which people keep at home, for example, a cat or dog), sale (how much a company sells), brand (the name for products of one company). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Study finds majority of pilots nod off mid-flight
items.text: A new report has raised serious concerns about pilot fatigue. The European Cockpit Association (ECA) conducted a survey of nearly 7,200 pilots across 32 countries. It discovered that exhaustion in the cockpit is a widespread and underreported problem. More than three-quarters of respondents said they had briefly dozed off while operating an aircraft in the month before the survey. Almost a quarter of them admitted they continued flying even when they were too tired. Furthermore, half said they had operated a flight when they should have declared themselves unfit for duty. Tiredness can result from long working hours, insufficient rest, and unpredictable schedules. The pilots were very frank in their answers to the survey questions. Many said they were reluctant to report fatigue because they feared punishment or other negative reactions from their bosses. Captain Coen George, a director of the ECA, warned: "When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit." Aviation safety experts say exhaustion can impair judgement, slow reaction times and prevent pilots from responding effectively to unexpected in-flight situations. The experts urged airlines to foster a culture in which pilots can report tiredness without fear of repercussions. Carriers should ensure that passenger safety is their top priority. items.title: World-famous London shopping street pedestrianized
items.text: One of London's most famous shopping streets has been pedestrianized. This means no cars, buses, trucks, or motorbikes can enter it. The street is called Oxford Street. It is well known all over the world. It used to be full of traffic. The Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, decided to make it pedestrian-only. Around one kilometre of the street is off limits to vehicles. However, delivery trucks can use the area between midnight and 7 am. Mayor Khan hopes the pedestrianization will bring more shoppers back to the area. He called it a very important event for London. Mr Khan also plans to plant more trees along the street, create public squares, and add more seats and tables. There have been mixed reactions to the pedestrianization of Oxford Street. Many people support the plan. They are happy that the area will be less polluted. Khan said a traffic-free Oxford Street would "unlock the full potential" of an important area of London and help make a better, greener, and richer London. Around half a million people visit the street every day. However, many Londoners are unhappy that the street has been closed to traffic. Local official Tim Barnes said: "Traffic will be pushed to the small streets nearby causing economic and environmental harm." The Spectator magazine warned that life for car drivers would be harder. items.title: Mummy removed from exhibition over 'lack of consent'
items.text: A museum in Scotland has removed the remains of an ancient Egyptian mummy from an exhibition because there is no documented evidence that the deceased gave consent for their remains to be displayed. Glasgow's Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum took away the remains of a priest named Nakht, a mummified male head, and other body parts. In place of the exhibits, visitors found signs explaining that the remains had been removed "as a mark of respect". The museum said the decision "reflects contemporary museum practice". It added: "In the absence of consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." The decision has provoked widespread criticism. Scottish politician Murdo Fraser called the move "woke madness". He argued that museums should showcase history rather than hide it. A museum visitor complained that his daughter was upset at not being able to see the exhibits. An education campaigner said the decision "represents the triumph of educational stupidity and ignorance". He added: "It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago." However, the museum defended its action. items.title: Man sells everything for AI dream "partner"
items.text: A man in Brazil had a sad experience in his search for love. Mr X, 49, sold everything he owned to get enough money to see a woman he met online. He travelled over 2,000 kilometres by bus. He first met her online in 2020 and fell in love with her. He wanted to marry her. Her name was Jessica. Her online profile read: "I really want to support you. I want you to come to my farm and never work again in your life." Mr X went to meet her in the city of Belo Horizonte, but he could not find her. He showed people photos of her, but nobody knew who she was. He then found out that she was not real. She was created by AI. The man was sad. He said: "I came here to find happiness." Mr X's story shows how risky it can be to look for love online. Many people feel lonely and want to find a partner. However, they can be easily tricked because AI can make people who look and sound real. Jessica's social media account had over 300,000 followers. She looked like a real woman. The person who created Jessica said they made her to get people's attention online. They wanted to use the AI Jessica to help sell things. Mr X wants people to be careful so they don't make a similar mistake in the future. It is important to check the identity of a person you meet online carefully. items.title: Influencers in Mexico work for drug groups
items.text: Ever since the Sinaloa Cartel split into rival groups in 2024, social media has turned into a dangerous battleground for Mexico’s drug wars. The competing factions regularly target popular content creators, and use them to show off power, post propaganda , and recruit young people. Local influencers who adopt narco culture for clicks often get caught in the middle and put themselves directly in the sights of rival gangs. On top of that, federal agents are looking into dozens of creators accused of helping cartels clean dirty money through online shops, brand deals, and live donations. This deadly connection has already cost the lives of at least 19 influencers across the country. Weak police work, a lack of real punishment, and slow moderation by tech platforms mean cartels can keep using young creators as easy tools for cash and influence online. Difficult words: faction (a small, organized group within a larger organization or political party), propaganda (information, ideas, or rumors deliberately spread to influence public opinion or promote a political cause), lack (not enough of something). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Influencers in Mexico work for drug groups
items.text: In Mexico, social media is a dangerous battleground for drug cartels. Since a big cartel split into fighting groups in 2024, criminal gangs use popular influencers for propaganda , showing off power, and attracting young members. At least 19 internet stars died after being linked to criminal organizations. Some influencers make videos about drug culture for clicks, while others are investigated for helping cartels clean illegal money through private businesses and shops. Police struggle to stop the violence, and very few murders are ever solved. Social media companies try to ban bad profiles, but cartels use hidden codes to break rules. As a result, young influencers are still in danger. Difficult words: battleground (a place where a fight or war takes place), cartel (a large group of criminals), propaganda (information used to make people believe a certain idea or group). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Influencers in Mexico work for drug groups
items.text: Drug gangs in Mexico are using social media. They want to show off and fight each other. Back in 2024, a big gang breaks into two groups. Now, they are fighting for control. They use young online stars to make videos and bring in new people. But this is very dangerous. At least 19 creators die. Some creators talk about gang life only to get views. Others help hide dirty money in normal businesses. The police do not stop the killers. The danger keeps growing. Social media companies try to block bad accounts, but it is not enough to keep young people safe. Difficult words: show off (to show something proudly to make others like or support you), hide (to put something in a place where nobody can see it), danger (a situation when something bad may happen). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Canada and Europe want to work closer together
items.text: A summit in Montreal has highlighted a growing push to deepen political and economic ties between Canada and the EU. Motivated by trade disputes, geopolitical friction , and economic pressures from the United States, many Canadians are actively favoring European trade over American imports. While European Commission leadership proposed the idea of making Canada an associate member , major member states like France and Germany remain hesitant due to treaty limits and undefined legal terms. Despite these political hurdles, practical integration is already accelerating across some sectors. Canada has joined joint defense procurement programs and is exploring agreements covering energy, critical raw materials, and student exchanges. Both Canadian and European leaders view this closer partnership as essential for protecting national sovereignty, reducing dangerous dependencies on global superpowers, and securing critical supply chains in an increasingly unstable global economy. Difficult words: friction (disagreement, conflict, or tension between people or groups with different views), associate member (a member of an organization or group who has limited rights or status compared to full members), procurement (obtaining or buying goods and services, especially for a government or organization). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Canada and Europe want to work closer together
items.text: Canada and the EU are working to build a much stronger partnership. Because of trade problems and rising costs with the United States, many Canadians prefer to buy goods from Europe and support local businesses. European leaders discussed giving Canada a special status , but some countries like Germany and France say the rules are not clear yet. Even without a formal title, Canada and the EU are already working closer together on important projects. They are sharing plans for defense , energy, clean technology, and student programs. Both sides believe that building strong relationships outside of North America will help protect their economy, keep energy supplies safe, and make their nations stronger for the future. Difficult words: status (the official position of a person, country, or organization), defense (protecting a country, building, or person against attack or harm), supply (an amount of something available to be used). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Canada and Europe want to work closer together
items.text: Canada and Europe want to work closer together. Many people in Canada prefer to buy things from Europe instead of the United States. Trade with the United States is changing. European leaders are talking about how to help each other more. They want to share energy, keep prices low, and help students study in different countries. Some big countries in Europe say that the rules are not ready for a special membership . But they still want to be strong friends. Working together helps both Canada and Europe stay safe, protect their businesses, and keep their people happy. Difficult words: share (to give a part of something to others, or to use something together), membership (when a country or person belongs to a group, club, or organization), protect (to keep someone or something safe). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Who will be the next James Bond?
items.text: Reports indicate that final auditions are currently underway to select the next James Bond. Actors Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Callum Turner emerge as top contenders . Screen tests are reportedly evaluating finalists across three critical criteria: stunt capabilities, dialogue performance, and overall screen presence. Industry analysts highlight Jack Lowden as the current betting favorite and note his potential for a dramatic character transformation. Meanwhile, Josh O’Connor brings acclaimed dramatic experience, and Callum Turner offers a classic, retro aesthetic. Experts also suggest that studio executives might still surprise audiences by choosing an unexpected actor, such as Jacob Elordi. The rigorous selection process aims to ensure the new 007 appeals to a global audience under Amazon MGM Studios, with an official announcement expected around Christmas. Difficult words: contender (a person who competes for a position, prize, or title), stunt (an action that requires physical skill and strength, performed to entertain people in a film or show), acclaimed (publicly praised or celebrated), rigorous (extremely thorough, careful, and demanding strict adherence to standards). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Who will be the next James Bond?
items.text: Actors Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Callum Turner are reportedly in the final auditions to play the next James Bond. Testing involves three main parts: performing stunts , delivering dialogue, and showing strong screen presence . Jack Lowden is currently the favorite among betting groups, though all three actors bring special styles to the famous role. Experts say that producers want a British or Commonwealth actor, though a surprise candidate could still be selected. Studio executives hope to make a press announcement around Christmas to reveal the new 007 actor to fans worldwide. Difficult words: audition (a short performance by an actor, singer, or dancer to show their ability for a role), stunt (a dangerous or difficult action done in a movie), screen presence (when an actor can get the audience’s attention whenever they appear on camera). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
